title: Max your IRA — Roth or Traditional based on your bracket
summary: $7,500 for 2026 ($8,600 if 50+). Lower fees, broader fund selection than most 401(k) plans.
detailsHtml:
Why max the IRA before going further on the 401(k)

Most 401(k) plans have fund expense ratios 2–10x higher than what's available in a self-directed IRA. Over 30 years, a 0.5% annual fee differential compounds to roughly a 15% smaller terminal balance. After capturing the match, the IRA is generally a better next dollar.

${bracketBlock( 'Roth IRA, unambiguously. You\'ll almost certainly be in a higher bracket in retirement than you are today. Pay 10–12% tax now and watch the balance grow tax-free for decades.', 'The choice depends on your retirement projection. If you expect to be in the same or higher bracket in retirement (high savings rate, pension, rental income), Roth wins. If you expect a lower bracket (typical for most Americans who don\'t save aggressively), Traditional wins. Splitting contributions hedges the uncertainty.', 'You are likely above the Roth IRA direct contribution income limits. For 2026, the phase-out is $153,000–$168,000 (single) and $242,000–$252,000 (married filing jointly). Above the upper end, direct contributions are prohibited. Use the backdoor Roth IRA: contribute to a non-deductible Traditional IRA, then convert immediately to Roth. The pro-rata rule complicates this if you have existing pre-tax Traditional IRA balances; consult a fiduciary tax advisor (apply the fiduciary-vs-suitability test on the Welcome view before engaging) before executing.' )}
2026 IRA limits: $7,500 standard $8,600 with catch-up (age 50+) IRA catch-up now inflation-indexed (first increase since 2006)
Saver's Credit (IRC §25B) — the under-claimed credit for low/moderate-income contributors. If your AGI is below the §25B thresholds — for 2026 $24,250 single / $36,375 head of household / $48,500 MFJ at the 50% credit tier, with reduced tiers (20% and 10%) phasing through $26,250 / $39,375 / $52,500 (single/HoH/MFJ) and out around $40,250 / $60,375 / $80,500 (2026, IRS Notice 2025-67) — your IRA or 401(k) contribution earns a nonrefundable credit on top of the deductibility benefit. The credit is 50%, 20%, or 10% of the first $2,000 contributed ($4,000 MFJ). At the 50% tier a $2,000 IRA contribution produces a $1,000 federal tax credit, on top of the Traditional-IRA deduction at your marginal rate — an effectively guaranteed return that exceeds nearly every other optimization lever in this framework. The credit is documented as massively under-claimed (IRS participation is roughly one-third of theoretical eligibility per Pew / Brookings research). File IRS Form 8880 to claim it. Verify the year's exact AGI thresholds against the IRS Rev. Proc. before filing — they index annually. Horizon note: SECURE 2.0 §103 replaces this credit with the Saver's Match beginning tax year 2027 — a 50% federal match on up to $2,000 of retirement contributions (max $1,000), deposited directly into the saver's retirement account rather than credited on the return. The contribute-then-claim behavior carries over; the payoff mechanics change.
